# R4 Digest — Weima BECNT: 1 Thess 4:1–18 (Holiness, Philadelphia, Parousia)

**Source slice:** `.cache/weima-thessalonians-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R4_1th_holiness_parousia_3418-4163.txt`  
**Raw lines:** 3418–4163  
**Range coverage:** IV. Exhortations intro + A. Increasing in conduct that pleases God (4:1–12) + B. Comfort concerning deceased Christians at Christ’s return (4:13–18). Slice ends after 4:18 additional notes; 5:1–11 is next range.  
**Attribution:** All interpretive claims are Weima’s unless noted as his report of other scholars (Plevnik, Harnisch/Schmithals, Cosby, Peterson, dispensational rapture, etc.).  
**Overflow / boundary flags:** Section C (5:1–11) is outlined and compared for structure but **not** fully expounded in-range; do not treat 5:1–11 as covered. R5 continues Day of the Lord / congregational material.

## A. Literary frame: paraenetic half of the letter (4:1–5:22)

### C-R4-01
**Claim:** At 4:1 Paul shifts from the apologetic purpose of 2:1–3:13 (defending past mission conduct and present absence) to the exhortative purpose of 4:1–5:22, fulfilling the desire to “complete the things that are lacking in [their] faith” (3:10) via Timothy’s report (3:6): sexual/conduct holiness (4:1–12), comfort over deceased at the parousia (4:13–18), comfort for the living (5:1–11), congregational life (5:12–22).
**Quote:** “A major shift in the body of the letter takes place at 4:1 as Paul has now completed the apologetic purpose that characterizes the first half (2:1–3:13) and moves on to the exhortative purpose at work throughout the second half (4:1–5:22).”
**Locus:** Intro to IV; 1 Thess 4:1–5:22 structure
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R4-02
**Claim:** 4:1–12 (and the second half generally) is **paraenesis**—traditional moral/religious exhortation on practical living. Weima rejects Dibelius-style “stock topoi with no real situation” for 4:1–12: specificity of 3b–6a and 10b–12, strategic placement, threatening tone of 6b–8, and Gentile sexual laxity show Paul addresses a real Thessalonian situation tied to Timothy’s report and “things lacking” (3:10).
**Quote:** “Most scholars today, however, recognize that Paul has used the source materials for his paraenesis with great care, modifying them so that they better relate to the specific historical situation that he is addressing. This also appears to be the case in 1 Thess. 4:1–12.”
**Locus:** Literary Analysis, Character of the Passage; 4:1–12
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[paul-apostle]]

### C-R4-03
**Claim:** Coherence of 4:1–12 (vs. major breaks at 4:8 or 4:10a): three inclusios (walk / “increase more and more” / “commands”) bind 1–12; material is previously shared (contrast unique disclosure form at 4:13); common theme is walking in a way that pleases God. *Peri de* at 4:9 and appeal at 4:10b mark **minor** subunits.
**Quote:** “Three inclusios… exist within the opening and closing verses of 4:1–12… The coherence of 4:1–12 is further evident in that the exhortations given in this passage all constitute previously shared material.”
**Locus:** Extent / Structure of 4:1–12
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-04
**Claim:** Structure of 4:1–12: (1) Introduction 1–2; (2) Holiness in sexual conduct 3–8 = thesis 3a + three exhortations 3b–6a + three reasons 6b–8 (Lord Jesus as avenger / past call of God / present gift of the Spirit); (3) Love for one another 9–12 = general affirmation 9–10a + specific appeal 10b–12 with purpose clause 12.
**Quote:** “The structure of 4:1–12, therefore, is as follows: 1. Introduction (4:1–2) 2. Holiness in sexual conduct (4:3–8) … 3. Love for one another (4:9–12)”
**Locus:** Structure of the Passage; 4:1–12
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

## B. Introduction: increase in God-pleasing conduct (4:1–2)

### C-R4-05
**Claim:** *Loipon oun* (“and so”) is unique in the NT; Weima prefers a soft link to 3:10 and the prayer of 3:12–13 (not mere “finally” ending the letter, nor strong inference from 3:11–13 alone). Paul uses an **appeal formula** (*erōtōmen kai parakaloumen*) with friendlier tone than “command,” yet “in the Lord Jesus” grounds authority as representative of Jesus.
**Quote:** “The rendering of *loipon oun* as ‘and so’ (Moule 1959: 161) more accurately expresses the somewhat veiled nature of the link… Even though the appeal formula conveys a friendly and less heavy-handed tone, Paul still speaks authoritatively… ‘in the Lord Jesus.’”
**Locus:** 4:1
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-06
**Claim:** “You received… how you must walk and so please God”: *paralambanō* is technical for transmission of tradition (stronger rabbinic parallel); *peripatein* = moral conduct (Jewish background, intelligible to Gentiles); *kai* consecutive—please God is purpose/result of walking. Paraenesis cannot be separated from kerygma; sociological identity-formation is real but motivation is also theological “pleasing God” as covenant-boundary marker (Weima 1996).
**Quote:** “For the apostle, paraenesis cannot be separated from kerygma… The apostle’s motivation, however, is not solely sociological but also stems from his theological conviction that ‘pleasing God’… is the defining characteristic that distinguishes members of the covenant community from those who are of the world.”
**Locus:** 4:1–2
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-07
**Claim:** Content of the appeal is “that you increase more and more” in walking that pleases God—general enough to theme 4:1–12. V. 2’s “commands… through the Lord Jesus” (*parangelia* with military/magisterial force) adds authoritative emphasis; greater expectation attaches to previously taught material than to new topics (e.g., fate of the dead, 4:13–18).
**Quote:** “Consequently, there is a greater degree of expectation on the apostle’s part that they fulfill this appeal compared to other matters on which they have not yet been taught (e.g., the fate of deceased believers at Christ’s return, taken up in 4:13–18).”
**Locus:** 4:1–2
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

## C. Holiness in sexual conduct (4:3–8) — will of God, porneia, vessel, Spirit, avenger

### C-R4-08
**Claim:** Greco-Roman sexual laxity (Demosthenes, Cato, Cicero, Plutarch; concubinage, prostitution, Augustus’s failed Julian Laws) and cultic sexuality at Thessalonica (Cabirus phallic ritual; Dionysus; Isis/Aphrodite) frame Paul’s concern that Gentile converts not revert under social pressure (affliction = social harassment for leaving cults, not primarily physical martyrdom).
**Quote:** “In light of the general sexual laxity and promiscuity practiced throughout the ancient Greco-Roman world—as well as the sexual component in a number of the pagan religions of the day, particularly in the most popular cults of Thessalonica—we can better appreciate Paul’s concern in 1 Thess. 4:3–8…”
**Locus:** Historical context for 4:3–8
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-09
**Claim (thesis):** “This—namely, your holiness—is the will of God” (*hagiasmos* in apposition to *touto*). Fourfold holy-root in 3–8 (noun 3×; “Spirit… holy” in 8) plus foreshadowing in 3:13 and expanded peace benediction 5:23. Holiness is Israel’s covenant boundary marker (Exod 19; Deut 26; Lev Holiness Code; Pharisaic “separated ones”); astonishingly Paul applies it to predominantly Gentile Thessalonians as **renewed Israel**—holiness now separates them from “Gentiles who do not know God” (4:5) and “outsiders” (4:12).
**Quote:** “What is surprising and even astonishing, however, is that Paul applies this standard of holiness to predominantly Gentile believers in Jesus at Thessalonica… Paul, it seems clear, views his Gentile converts at Thessalonica as the renewed Israel… And on the basis of their privileged new position, he exhorts them in 4:3–8 to exhibit the holiness that God’s people have always been called to possess.”
**Locus:** 4:3a (with Weima 1996)
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-10
**Claim (exhortation 1):** “Separate yourselves from sexual immorality” (*apechesthai… apo tēs porneias*) plays on holiness-as-separation. *Porneia* = umbrella for sexual misconduct (pre/extramarital, homosexual activity), not narrow fornication-only or incest/forbidden kinship; broad sense fits general intro plus “lustful passion” (v. 5) and “impurity” (v. 7). Minority Stoic fidelity voices existed; mainstream was tolerance.
**Quote:** “Most scholars, however, understand *porneia* to refer in a general way to all kinds of sexual misconduct, including both premarital and extramarital sex as well as homosexual activity… This broad understanding of the term best fits the context…”
**Locus:** 4:3b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-11
**Claim (*skeuos / ktasthai* debate):** Three main options for 4:4: (1) acquire a wife; (2) live sexually with one’s wife; (3) control one’s body/sex organ. Weima finds (3) strongest with fewest objections; prefers translating *skeuos* literally as “vessel” to preserve ambiguity (body vs genitalia). Supports for body/genitalia: 1 Sam 21:5 LXX, 4Q416, secular euphemisms, Cabirus/Dionysus phallic cults, Pauline body language. Intent: all Christians, single or married, control sexual urges “in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion.”
**Quote:** “Nevertheless, the interpretation that has the strongest support and the fewest objections is the third: ‘that each one of you know how to control his own body/sex organ’… it is perhaps wisest to translate the noun *skeuos* with its literal meaning of ‘vessel.’”
**Locus:** 4:4–5
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-12
**Claim:** “In holiness and honor” is other-centered respect (opposite self-centered lust); “in lustful passion” (*en pathei epithymias*, qualitative genitive). Comparative clause “just as also the Gentiles who do not know God” roots immorality in ignorance of God (OT + Rom 1:24–28) and places the verse in **covenant** frame (“to know God”). Striking antithesis: Gentile Christians must not act sexually like Gentiles—they have a new identity as covenant people; holiness in sexual conduct is boundary marker.
**Quote:** “Why does Paul tell Gentile Christians in Thessalonica to stop acting in their sex life like Gentiles? The apostle’s statement does make sense, however, if he no longer views these converts as Gentiles but with a new identity: they are now members of God’s covenant people.”
**Locus:** 4:4–5
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-13
**Claim (exhortation 3):** “That one not trespass or take advantage of his brother in this matter” remains **sexual**, not commercial/business (rejects Calvin et al.). Reasons against business reading: no transition formula; single sentence with sexual infinitives; lexical holiness coherence of 3–8; *akatharsia* sexual. *Hyperbainein* = sexual trespass beyond holiness/honor; *pleonektein* = deceptive advantage; *en tō pragmati* = “in this matter” / likely euphemism for illicit sexual affair. Likely illicit sexual conduct with another believer’s household women (patriarchal address to males), not primarily homosexual acts with the “brother.”
**Quote:** “It appears clear, therefore, that the rather ambiguous words in the third exhortation… ought to be interpreted as giving further instruction dealing with holiness in sexual conduct rather than with a new subject of proper business practices… it is more likely that the apostle has in view the illicit sexual conduct of a male believer with either the wife, daughter, or another female member belonging to the extended household of his fellow Christian.”
**Locus:** 4:6a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-14
**Claim (reason 1 — future judgment):** “Because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things.” *Kyrios* = Jesus (not God), given consistent use in the letter, redundancy if “God” follows, and Jesus as agent of eschatological wrath in Thessalonians. *Ekdikos* = just punishment, not vindictive “revenge.” Parenthetical *kathōs*: already told and solemnly warned—third reminder of prior teaching, increasing culpability.
**Quote:** “Against this conclusion [that *kyrios* = God], however, are at least three factors… Third, throughout both Thessalonian Letters, Paul makes several references to the future coming of Jesus, who will punish the wicked and serve as the agent of God’s wrath…”
**Locus:** 4:6b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]]

### C-R4-15
**Claim (reason 2 — past call):** “God did not call us for impurity but in holiness.” Aorist of initial conversion call; *epi akatharsia* = purpose/result “for impurity” (sexual); shift to *en hagiasmō* significant—not merely parallel purpose (*epi*/*eis*) but state/condition: holiness as past-and-present reality begun at conversion (third *hagiasmos* recalling thesis 3a).
**Quote:** “If Paul here in 1 Thess. 4:7 similarly is referring to the state or condition of the Thessalonians at their calling, his point is that holiness is not so much a future goal as a past and present reality—a state of holiness that started already at their conversion and continues in their current lives.”
**Locus:** 4:7
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-16
**Claim (reason 3 — present Spirit gift):** Emphatic *toigaroun*: rejecting the sexual exhortations rejects not a human (Paul) but God “who indeed gives his Spirit, who is holy, into you.” Word order stresses Spirit’s holy character. Deliberate echo of new-covenant/messianic Spirit promises (esp. Ezek 36:25–27; 37:6, 14 LXX *eis hymas*); present participle *didonta* = ongoing reality, not future only. Gentile conversion = fulfillment of Israel’s eschatological promises; Spirit empowers holy living. Triadic pattern (not necessarily conscious): future Lord Jesus / past God / present Holy Spirit.
**Quote:** “Paul takes this new-covenant language, which articulates the eschatological hope of the Jewish people, and applies it to Gentile Christians at Thessalonica… for Paul it has become a present and ongoing reality, as indicated by the present tense of the participle *didonta*… So here, as elsewhere in Paul’s Letters, the Holy Spirit is the power that enables believers to live holy lives.”
**Locus:** 4:8
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]

## D. Philadelphia and quiet work (4:9–12)

### C-R4-17
**Claim:** Second way to increase God-pleasing conduct = mutual love, foreshadowed in 3:12. Link to prior unit may be “wronging a brother” (6a) ↔ idleness as violation of *philadelphia*. Structure: affirmation 9–10a + appeal 10b–12. Fourth exhortation “work with your hands” is most prominent (parenthetical prior command; purpose clause echoes self-sufficiency; progressive specificity). Affirmation of mutual love functions as corrective foil to idleness exploiting generosity.
**Quote:** “This observation that Paul is especially concerned with the problem of idleness in the specific appeal of 4:10b–12 impacts how one ought to read the general affirmation of verses 9–10a… the refusal of some in the church to work but instead take advantage of the generosity of fellow believers is a clear violation of the call for Christians to love one another.”
**Locus:** Intro to 4:9–12
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-18
**Claim:** *Peri de* introduces new topic from Timothy’s **oral** report, not necessarily a Thessalonian letter (contra Milligan/Frame/Malherbe et al.; cf. Mitchell 1989). *Philadelphia* = figurative mutual love among male and female believers (inclusive sibling image); powerful Greco-Roman solidarity image. “No need to write” = **paraleipsis** (commendation, not literal refusal to address).
**Quote:** “Since there is no explicit reference to a letter from the Thessalonians (as there is in 1 Cor. 7:1), it is better to conclude that *peri de* introduces a new subject that Paul raises in response to the oral report of Timothy (3:6)… Rather, Paul’s opening assertion is an example of *paraleipsis*…”
**Locus:** 4:9a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-19
**Claim (*theodidaktoi*):** Hapax-like coinage “taught by God.” Weima rejects Koester (self-reliance), Malherbe (anti-Epicurean autodidaktos), Roetzel (Hellenistic-Jewish release from work), Kloppenborg (Dioscuri as models of *philadelphia*). Majority/Weima: allusion to Isa 54:13 and broader eschatological divine-instruction hope (Jer 31; Isa 2; Mic 4; Pss. Sol. 17.32; John 6:45; 1 John 2:27)—new-covenant blessing extended to Gentile Thessalonians as renewed Israel. Agent of teaching: Holy Spirit (link to 4:8; cf. 1 Cor 2:13); purpose: “to love one another.”
**Quote:** “Paul’s use of the term *theodidaktoi*, therefore, is significant… suggests that here too Paul views the Thessalonians’ practice of *philadelphia*, or mutual love, as an eschatological blessing of God’s covenant people… The Spirit’s role in teaching… strongly suggests that the apostle has in mind the Holy Spirit’s role in teaching and empowering believers…”
**Locus:** 4:9b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]

### C-R4-20
**Claim:** Second reason they need no writing: they already practice love “to all the brothers in the whole of Macedonia” (not mere hyperbole). Most likely **economic aid** to needy Macedonian Christians (2 Cor 8:1–2 poverty; fits “all”; prepares “work… need of no one”), rather than primarily evangelism support or hospitality to travelers.
**Quote:** “A third and more likely possibility, however, is that Paul alludes here to the economic aid that the Thessalonians were providing for needy Christians within their region.”
**Locus:** 4:10a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-21
**Claim (appeals 1–3):** (1) “Increase more and more” = abound in *philadelphia* (cf. 3:12; balances later work command as 2 Thess 3:13 balances idleness rebuke). (2) “Make it your ambition to live a quiet life” (*philotimeisthai hēsychazein*): free from meddling/busybody disturbance (clarified by 2 Thess 3:11–12). (3) “Mind your own business” (*prassein ta idia*): classical pairing with quiet life (Plato, Dio Cassius). Weima: evidence too thin for confident political-demos, patron-client, or aggressive-evangelism reconstructions; default = low public profile + *philadelphia* within church to minimize opposition.
**Quote:** “Most commentators, therefore, settle for understanding Paul’s exhortation ‘to live a quiet life’ in a more general manner… maintain a low profile in the public arena, keep to themselves as much as possible, and practice *philadelphia* within the church, thereby minimizing the danger of arousing further opposition to the Christian movement.”
**Locus:** 4:10b–11b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-22
**Claim (appeal 4 + causes of idleness):** “Work with your hands” = literal manual labor; majority of church artisans/unskilled laborers; targets unwillingness to work (cf. 2 Thess 3:10), not inability. Cause debate: traditional **eschatological excitement** (imminent parousia → work “waste of time”) vs sociological (upper-class disdain for labor; patron-client freeloading). Weima: evidence insufficient for certainty, but if forced, eschatological argument slightly more convincing (idleness frames 4:13–5:11; heightened parousia expectation in both letters; historical analogues); early command against idleness does not disprove early enthusiasm. *Kathōs… commanded* likely stresses at least the work command.
**Quote:** “Nevertheless, if one is forced to make a decision, the eschatological argument seems to provide a slightly more convincing explanation than any of the sociological arguments for this state of affairs at Thessalonica.”
**Locus:** 4:11c
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]]

### C-R4-23
**Claim (purpose 4:12):** Dual purpose: (1) walk appropriately before **outsiders** (*tous exō*)—public reputation; theological holiness-as-boundary, not only pragmatic anti-persecution/evangelism; (2) “have need of no one” (masc. preferred)—personal responsibility, not autonomous disregard for others. Self-sufficient work is boundary marker parallel to sexual holiness vs “Gentiles who do not know God.”
**Quote:** “As full members of God’s covenant people, Gentile believers at Thessalonica are and must continue to be a holy community whose conduct in all aspects of life distinguishes them from the surrounding world.”
**Locus:** 4:12
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

## E. Comfort concerning the dead at Christ’s return (4:13–18)

### C-R4-24
**Claim:** 4:13–18 is hortatory/paraenetic despite didactic content: teaching aims to replace hopeless grief with comfort; disclosure + purpose clause + closing “comfort one another.” Distinct unit ending at 4:18 (not fused with 5:1–11) despite many formal parallels with 5:1–11 (Plevnik, Collins, Johanson, Howard, Luckensmeyer noted). Markers: *hōste* concluding clause; stereotyped “comfort one another”; thematic inclusio grief↔comfort; *peri de* + “brothers” at 5:1; 5:1–2 return to already-known material.
**Quote:** “These verses… do not interrupt Paul’s paraenesis, but are themselves hortatory… There can be little doubt, therefore, that 4:13–18 constitutes a distinct epistolary unit within 1 Thessalonians.”
**Locus:** Literary Analysis of 4:13–18
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-25
**Claim (structure):** (1) Opening assertion: Christians grieve with hope (13); (2) Reason 1: church confession (14); (3) Reason 2: “word of the Lord” (15–17: Pauline summary 15b + logion 16–17a + Pauline climax 17b); (4) Conclusion: comfort one another (18).
**Quote:** “Thus the structure of 4:13–18… is as follows: 1. Opening assertion… 2. Reason 1: The confession of the church (4:14) 3. Reason 2: The ‘word of the Lord’ (4:15–17) 4. Conclusion: Comfort one another (4:18)”
**Locus:** Structure of 4:13–18
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-26
**Claim (4:13 topic):** Disclosure form “we do not want you not to know” + brothers + *peri* marks **new, previously untaught** material (contrast repeated “you know / we commanded” in 4:1–12; 5:2). Topic: “those who are asleep” (*koimaō* = death euphemism, not “soul sleep”; intermediate conscious blessedness elsewhere in NT). Deaths not likely martyrdoms (affliction = social harassment; Bruce; lack of martyr-praise). Source of topic: Timothy oral report, not a written questionnaire.
**Quote:** “The form of the disclosure formula used in 4:13 suggests that the apostle is about to present something new and previously not taught to the Thessalonians… Although the apostle had taught the Thessalonians about the bodily resurrection of believers, he did not provide them with sufficient details about the specific matter of how the resurrection of these deceased believers coordinates with the event of Christ’s return…”
**Locus:** 4:13a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-27
**Claim (why grief — six hypotheses; Weima’s preferred):** Thesis: “that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope.” Hypotheses surveyed: (1) Gnostic “resurrection already” (Schmithals; Harnisch)—anachronistic/no evidence; (2) Paul had not yet taught resurrection (Marxsen, Lüdemann, Mearns, Nicholl)—incredible given 15+ years, creedal practice, Pharisee background; (3) theoretical belief collapses before actual death (Marshall, Green)—but focus is coordination with parousia; (4) abandoned confidence in second coming (Hyldahl)—letter thanks for ongoing hope; (5) **Plevnik/Lohfink assumption:** only living can be assumed to heaven—Weima: Gentile church unlikely steeped in that Jewish apocalyptic; also conflicts with *apantēsis* formal-reception image (movement to earth, not secret rapture/assumption to heaven); (6) **preferred:** fear that the dead are at a **disadvantage** relative to the living at the parousia (coordination problem).
**Quote:** “A sixth and most likely explanation is that the Thessalonians’ confusion over how precisely the one eschatological event involving the resurrection of deceased believers coordinated with the other future event involving Christ’s return led to the fear that their fellow church members who had already died would be at some kind of disadvantage at the parousia compared to themselves, who were still alive.”
**Locus:** 4:13 (crux interpretum; Luckensmeyer noted)
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-28
**Claim (supports for disadvantage thesis):** (a) emphatic future negation “will certainly not precede” (15b); (b) sequence dead rise “first” then living (16–17; *prōton* clause-final); (c) *hama syn autois* early placement emphasizing equality; (d) intertestamental parallels that “those who are left are more blessed” (2 Esd/4 Ezra 13:24 etc.). Deep grief understandable given anticipation of parousia vindication and privileged *apantēsis* escort role.
**Quote:** “In such a context it is not hard to comprehend the grief that these Thessalonian believers had, believing that their fellow church members who died before Christ’s return would be at some kind of disadvantage compared to themselves, who expected to be still alive at this glorious event.”
**Locus:** 4:13 with 15–17
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-29
**Claim (grief with hope, not absolute ban on grief):** Majority from Augustine/Theodoret: Paul does **not** forbid all grief (contra Lightfoot/Milligan/Frame/Best/Malherbe absolute reading of *kathōs*). Support: Phil 2:27; Rom 12:15; death as last enemy; Jesus weeping. Critical difference: outsiders grieve without hope (popular despair on inscriptions, Theocritus, Catullus, Irene’s P.Oxy. 115 vs Paul’s “with these words”); philosophers/mysteries’ afterlife hopes not widely popular (MacMullen).
**Quote:** “But while both non-Christians and Christians grieve at the death of loved ones, there is a critical difference: in contrast to the hopelessness that characterizes those outside the faith, believers grieve with hope.”
**Locus:** 4:13b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-30
**Claim (reason 1 — creed, 4:14):** “Since we believe that Jesus died and rose” (first-class *ei* = assumed true) cites pared creedal formula: *pisteuomen hoti* as creed intro; rare bare “Jesus”; rare *anistēmi* (vs Paul’s *egeirō*); Jesus as subject rising (vs God raising); economy of words. Rhetorical force: church-wide authority. Implication: Jesus’ resurrection guarantees deceased believers will be resurrected and present so God “will bring with him those who have fallen asleep”—problem is coordination/presence at parousia, not denial of resurrection.
**Quote:** “The logical link… is clear: the resurrection of Jesus functions as the guarantee of the resurrection of deceased believers such that they will be alive and with Jesus at his return… the problem at Thessalonica was not a denial of believers’ resurrection but an uncertainty of how this event coordinated with the parousia of Christ.”
**Locus:** 4:14
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-31
**Claim (*dia tou Iēsou* and destination):** “Through Jesus” modifies the verb “will bring,” not “those who have fallen asleep” (not “sleep in Jesus” ≈ *en Christō*); agency via Christ’s resurrection (cf. 1 Cor 15:21). Climactic “with him” (*syn autō*) matches 4:17 and 5:10. Locale: not heavenly assumption (Plevnik et al.) but, with *apantēsis*, gathering to escort Christ on remainder of journey **to earth**; fits cosmic renewal hope (Rom 8:19–22; 2 Pet 3; Rev 21).
**Quote:** “The language and imagery that Paul employs in this passage is not that of an assumption but of an official visit by a king or high-ranking official… The picture, then, is one in which both resurrected… and transformed… believers are gathered together to meet Jesus on the clouds in the air, where they proceed to escort him on the remainder of his journey to earth.”
**Locus:** 4:14 (preview of 17)
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-32
**Claim (“word of the Lord,” 4:15):** *Touto* is cataphoric to 15–17. Segmentation: Pauline summary 15b; Jesus logion loosely in 16–17a; Pauline conclusion 17b. Source options: agraphon; Synoptic paraphrase (esp. Matt 24; also 25:1–13); general Jesus end-time teaching; prophetic “word of the LORD.” Weima leans to **Jesus material** (Paul distinguishes his teaching from the Lord’s elsewhere; multiple Gospel echoes; S. Kim). Purpose: highest authority for the living-not-preceding-dead assertion—problem is significant enough to need creed + Jesus-word.
**Quote:** “By placing his assurance that the living would not have precedence over the dead at the coming of the Lord under the rubric ‘a word of the Lord,’ Paul attributed the highest possible authority to his assertion in v. 15b.”
**Locus:** 4:15
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-33
**Claim (summary 15b):** Emphatic “we who are alive, who are left until the *parousia* of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep.” *Ou mē* + aor. subj. is strongest negation; rare and emphatic in Paul (4× non-LXX); “sounds like a denial of an opinion actually held.” *Phthanō* here uniquely = “precede.” “We” does **not** prove Paul expected to live until the parousia (purpose is equal participation; “we” qualified by participles; both states possible at 5:10; life-threatening career already). *Parousia* evokes imperial/royal visit, intensified next by *apantēsis*.
**Quote:** “There are insufficient grounds, therefore, for concluding from the ‘we’ in verse 15 that Paul expected to live until the parousia… This marks the third place in the letter… where Paul uses the term *parousia* to describe the ‘coming’ of Christ, thereby evoking the image of a royal visit by a Roman emperor or official.”
**Locus:** 4:15b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-34
**Claim (apocalyptic poetry, not blueprint):** 4:16–17 is the most explicit Pauline (and perhaps NT) sequence for the return, but Gaventa/Marshall/Calvin: poetic/symbolic apocalyptic language; distinguish meaning and referent; primary pastoral purpose is comfort (4:18), not a detailed predictive timetable.
**Quote:** “This passage has more in common with poetry than with blueprints… There is a danger, therefore, of reading this passage in a too-literal fashion, in which the main goal is to distinguish all the activities described here so that an exact timetable of future events emerges. This would involve a misuse of a text whose primary purpose is… to provide pastoral comfort.”
**Locus:** 4:16–17 intro
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-35
**Claim (stage 1 — descent with three accompaniments):** Causal *hoti*: Lord **himself** descends from heaven. Three *en*-phrases likely three parallel circumstances (not 2–3 explaining 1): (1) commanding shout (*keleusma*)—most naturally Christ’s, aimed at dead to rise (John 5:25–29); (2) voice of an archangel (possibly Michael if definite; indefinite also possible); (3) trumpet of God—eschatological signal linked to resurrection (1 Cor 15:52). Imperial-visit pomp marks the dead’s raising so they share the triumphal parousia.
**Quote:** “The sound of a trumpet, therefore, functions not only as a stereotyped sign of Jesus’s return but, more important for the specific concern of the Thessalonians, also marks the moment when their deceased members will be brought to life such that they can participate equally in Christ’s triumphal *parousia*.”
**Locus:** 4:16a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-36
**Claim (stage 2 — dead rise first):** Consecutive *kai*: “the dead in Christ will rise first.” Shift from sleep euphemism to *nekroi*; *en Christō* = died as Christians (intermediate-state nuances debated). No discussion of non-Christian dead or resurrection body—pastoral focus. *Prōton* clause-final + *epeita* emphasize order: dead not disadvantaged; they rise first **to earth**, then with living are taken up (not privilege of rising straight into air ahead of living forever).
**Quote:** “Far from missing out on that glorious event or suffering some kind of disadvantage compared to those who are still alive on that day, the deceased believers will rise ‘first’ and so be able to participate equally with living believers in the privilege of going up to meet the descending Lord and escorting him on the final leg of his return to earth.”
**Locus:** 4:16b
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-37
**Claim (*harpazō* / “rapture” language):** Stage 3: living “snatched up” (*harpagēsometha*) together with them (*hama syn autois*—equality stressed). Verb = sudden taking; positive sense of being caught up (cf. 2 Cor 12; apocalyptic ascents). **Not** intended to teach “a secret rapture of the church”; possible wordplay inverting funerary use of *harpazō/rapio* (death snatches the living → living snatched so as not to face death). Divine passive: God snatches; clouds = theophanic means (Danielic/Son of Man return imagery), not primarily location.
**Quote:** “Paul’s choice of *harpazō* was intended not to teach ‘a secret rapture of the church’ but rather to make a possible wordplay, since this term was often used by non-Christian writers to speak of life or the living being ‘snatched away’ by death.”
**Locus:** 4:17a
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-38
**Claim (*apantēsis* as Hellenistic formal reception — Peterson):** Purpose: “for a reception of the Lord” (*eis apantēsin tou kyriou*). Noun was technical for civic custom: leading citizens go out to welcome visiting king/official and escort him into the city (E. Peterson 1930). Context with *parousia* makes this background highly probable (Green; most commentators); Cosby’s objections answerable (Gundry). NT parallels: Acts 28:15; Matt 25:6. Chrysostom already used the royal-entry analogy (confident go out; condemned wait below).
**Quote:** “Since the context of this formal reception is the time of the royal *parousia* of the Lord (v. 15), there remains little doubt that this custom formed the background of this teaching… There is compelling evidence, therefore, that the third remaining occurrence of *eis apantēsin* by Paul here in 1 Thess. 4:17 also intends to link the description of Christ’s *parousia* with a Hellenistic formal reception.”
**Locus:** 4:17
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-39
**Claim (direction of movement — against secret rapture / pure heavenward assumption):** Meeting is “in the air” (space between heaven and earth). Primary stress is not demon-domain mastery (Morris et al.) nor final heavenly destination of believers. *Apantēsis* strongly implies, after the meeting, escort of the Lord on the **remainder of his descent to earth**. Combined with 4:14, trajectory is Christ-to-earth reception, not church whisked away in a secret rapture.
**Quote:** “The apostle is similarly not emphasizing the final destination of believers, though his use of *apantēsis* to evoke the image of a Hellenistic formal reception strongly implies that, once all Christians are taken up to meet the returning Lord ‘in the air,’ they will escort him on the remainder of his victorious descent to earth.”
**Locus:** 4:17
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-40
**Claim (climax 17b + conclusion 18):** Pauline summary (not part of the logion): “and so we will always be with the Lord”—equal eternal presence for living and dead; pastoral climax parallel to “with him” (14) and 5:10. *Hōste*: “Therefore comfort one another with these words”—paraenetic goal; “these words” = the two arguments (creed + word of the Lord). Contrast Irene’s consolation (comfort yourselves in helplessness) with comfort grounded in resurrection/parousia promises.
**Quote:** “These are the two reasons why the Thessalonians can now obey Paul’s concluding call to ‘comfort one another.’ These are the two reasons why, in contrast to the hopelessness or despair that characterizes the way that those outside the church face the death of others, Christians grieve for deceased believers with hope.”
**Locus:** 4:17b–18
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

## F. Engagement with rival readings (as Weima presents them)

### C-R4-41
**Claim (Plevnik):** Weima reports Plevnik (with Lohfink): Paul taught assumption to heaven of the living; only living can be assumed; resurrection restores earthly life so dead can be assumed with living. Weima rejects for (a) unlikely Jewish-apocalyptic assumption literacy in brief Gentile mission; (b) *apantēsis*/parousia formal-reception imagery moves toward earth, not assumption’s heavenward destination; (c) 4:14 “bring with him” + escort model.
**Quote:** “Also, the idea that Paul had taught the Thessalonians that they would be assumed or taken up to heaven is unlikely in light of the apostle’s depiction of Christ’s coming with the metaphor of a Hellenistic formal reception… This metaphor does not involve the movement of the church away from earth to heaven (the destination involved in assumption) but the reverse: the church meets the returning Christ in the air and escorts him the remainder of the way to his destination: earth.”
**Locus:** 4:13 hyp. 5; 4:14 destination; 4:17
**Targets:** [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-42
**Claim (Harnisch/Schmithals gnostic hypothesis):** Reported and rejected: gnostic teachers claimed resurrection already happened; deaths caused grief over exclusion from salvation. Weima: early developed gnosticism doubtful; no strong evidence at Thessalonica; Paul’s response is not aimed at denying denial of resurrection doctrine.
**Quote:** “It is questionable, however, whether gnosticism as a developed movement existed at this early date. And if it did, there is no compelling evidence for the presence of gnostic teachers in Thessalonica… Furthermore, it does not appear from the apostle’s response that the problem at Thessalonica involved a denial of the resurrection doctrine.”
**Locus:** 4:13 hyp. 1 (Harnisch 1973; Schmithals 1972)
**Targets:** [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-43
**Claim (dispensational / secret rapture readings):** Weima explicitly denies that *harpazō* teaches a secret rapture of the church; sequence is public descent with shout/archangel/trumpet, resurrection of dead, joint snatching for formal reception, escort to earth, always with the Lord. Timetable-blueprint reading of apocalyptic symbols is a pastoral misuse.
**Quote:** “Paul’s choice of *harpazō* was intended not to teach ‘a secret rapture of the church’… This would involve a misuse of a text whose primary purpose is, as its concluding exhortation indicates (4:18), to provide pastoral comfort.”
**Locus:** 4:16–18
**Targets:** [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[apocalyptic-literature]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

### C-R4-44
**Claim (developmental theories of Paul’s eschatology):** Against reading 4:13–18 as “early” parousia teaching before full resurrection doctrine (Lüdemann dating; Marxsen; Mearns): Paul knew Christian deaths earlier; mission message included Jesus’ resurrection linked to believers’ (1 Cor 15:3–8 logic); he can cite “dead in Christ will rise” without defining resurrection; Pharisee background already held resurrection.
**Quote:** “Yet it strains credibility to believe that Paul had never previously encountered the death of Christians during the more than fifteen years that had passed from his conversion to the writing of 1 Thessalonians.”
**Locus:** 4:13 hyp. 2
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[paul-apostle]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]]

## G. Cross-unit theological synthesis (within range)

### C-R4-45
**Claim:** Across 4:1–12 Weima’s load-bearing synthesis: Gentile Thessalonians = renewed Israel / eschatological covenant people enjoying new-covenant gifts (Spirit 4:8; God-taught love 4:9) and therefore bound to holiness boundary markers in sex (3–8) and *philadelphia*/self-sufficient work toward outsiders (9–12). 4:13–18 then supplies previously missing coordination of resurrection with parousia so hope can underwrite grief and mutual comfort—third concern foreshadowed in 3:12–13.
**Quote:** “The holiness that previously has been the exclusive privilege and calling of Israel has now also become God’s purpose for Gentiles at Thessalonica… After providing his Thessalonian readers with these two compelling reasons why they ought not to grieve… Paul concludes by exhorting the church to ‘comfort one another with these words’ (v. 18).”
**Locus:** 4:3–12 synthesis + 4:13–18 intro
**Targets:** [[1-thessalonians]], [[parousia-1-thess-4]], [[jeffrey-weima]], [[paul-apostle]], [[weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt]], [[apocalyptic-literature]]
